synopsis: The corpus links Griffith University’s haul-truck collision-avoidance research to reaction-time assumptions of 0.5–1 second borrowed from road research, citing Henry-Rogers (1960) [f3310]. A 2005 Griffith thesis combined a 0.5-second reaction time with braking to derive detection ranges of 15 m to the sides for people, 50 m to the rear and 100 m to the front [f6207]. Griffith’s 2005 Doppler-radar work used Monte Carlo simulation and a field demonstration, reporting light-vehicle detection at 75 m [f6368]. For planning, that observed detection distance must be distinguished from a braking trigger: the radar work was a detection study, not a brake-threshold study, while the reaction-time assumptions originated in road research [f6369, f3310].

relations.note: Specifies a 0.5-second assumption and the resulting directional detection ranges.
Clarifies that the reported 75 m detection result does not establish a brake threshold.
